claims.text: An aluminum-enriched interfacial transition layer can tune interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
Tuning interface coherency through aluminum enrichment shifts the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
As-deposited HEA multilayers have uncontrolled lattice mismatch and interface coherency.
The proposed intervention is controlled aluminum enrichment of the interfacial composition.
Elevated temperature and low-to-moderate stress are typical conditions for creep in protective coatings.
Aluminum enrichment reduces lattice mismatch at the HEA/interlayer boundary.
Reduced lattice mismatch optimizes interface coherency.
Aluminum addition modifies the lattice parameter at the interface.
Aluminum enrichment decreases vacancy- or atom-diffusion pathways at the interface.
Aluminum enrichment promotes dislocation nucleation and motion.
Changes in diffusional pathways and dislocation activity cause a transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep.
The creep rate and activation energy of Al-enriched samples will indicate a switch to dislocation-dominated creep relative to unmodified interfaces.
HEA multilayers without interfacial aluminum enrichment primarily exhibit diffusion-mediated creep.
The proposed transition occurs under high-temperature, low-to-moderate-stress conditions.
The transition may vary outside the tested thermal-stability or stress regime.
The aluminum concentration and spatial distribution required for optimal coherency are unknown.
The scalability of aluminum enrichment across different HEA compositions is unknown.
